subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF ADDITIONAL AGREEMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieith (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SIGNING OF ADDITIONAL AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement to the house at this time. In the past few days agreements under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act have been concluded with four additional provinces, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. As was the case with that signed earlier this month with Newfoundland, the effective date of these agreements is July 1. In view of the fact that royal assent has now been obtained for the amendment to the related federal legislation, the dominion government will therefore be in the position as of tomorrow to begin payments towards the cost of hospital insurance plans in these five provinces.
In other words, our objective of getting the program under way in all provinces wishing to participate as of July 1 has now been achieved. I think it is highly fitting that an undertaking of such importance to the people of Canada should be launched on the nation's birthday.
I might say that the basic agreement entered into in each case is substantially the same. As hon. members may know there are, however, areas of the act in which the provinces are permitted leeway in developing their programs. Accordingly certain differences occur in provincial plans, and these are reflected in the schedules of the agreements which have been completed.
In all cases the basic inpatient services enumerated in the federal act are provided for. In this connection the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta propose to impose an authorized charge. An authorized
charge is a levy made on an individual at the time a service is provided, and as far as British Columbia is concerned this will amount to $1 per day for hospital care. In Alberta the authorized charge will be $1 per day for new-born infants and from $1.50 to $2 per day for others, depending on the size of the hospital. The other three provinces are not imposing such charges.
With regard to outpatient services, the Manitoba and Saskatchewan plans will make these available on an emergency basis. In addition, Saskatchewan will provide for the pathological examination of tissue. The agreements with Alberta and British Columbia do not contain provisions for outpatient services. British Columbia, however, will continue to supply an emergency service to outpatients and will levy a $2 authorized charge in this connection. As previously indicated, Newfoundland proposes to furnish a fairly wide range of out-patient services.
Hon. members will recall that four of the five provinces now entering into shared programs with the federal authority have been operating provincial hospital insurance plans of one kind or another for the past few years. It is hoped that the support now available through the contributions of the dominion government will enable them to extend and improve further the hospital and diagnostic services which are available to their residents under this program.
On behalf of the dominion government and officials of my department I should like to thank these provinces which tomorrow will join with the dominion government in initiating this nation-wide program of hospital insurance for the fine spirit of co-operation which they have shown in bringing these agreements to completion. To me the pattern of joint effort developed in this connection augurs well for the future of this major federal-provincial undertaking in the health field. I am sure hon. members will join with me in wishing these five provinces success in directing their plans to the benefit of all their people.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON DROWNING OF FIVE MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 12 I made a statement to the house concerning the tragic accident on lake Simcoe on June 7 in which five members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police lost their lives. The statement appears at page 1064 of Hansard for that date.
Now that the inquest has been completed there are certain further observations I feel I should make to the house, particularly as there would seem to be some discrepancies between the facts contained in my previous statement and the evidence given at the inquest. That inquest was in form of an inquiry into the cause of the death of Corporal Smart, whose body was the only one recovered at that time, but it was in effect an inquiry into the cause and circumstances of this whole disaster.
In the first place I should like to read into the record the actual text of the finding of the coroner's jury:
We, the jury, find that Corporal Herbert Smart met his death by accidental drowning on lake Simcoe, off Georgina island, on the night of June the 7th, due to rough sea caused by storm, failure of motor, causing boat to swamp.
We, the jury, found by testimony and observation of test that boat on night in question was overloaded and also overcrowded, and at the same time, on our discussion, this plaque of Canadian Boating Federation Incorporated and Department of Transport is confusing of proper maximum weight.
With further regard, on observation of test made on Black river with two experienced swimmers, that we find the Department of Transport standard life jacket and approved Department of Transport life cushions to be unsatisfactory in case of emergency. Therefore, we, the jury, strongly recommend that a life jacket type vest is the most serviceable.
We, the jury, recommend that the plaque issued by the Canadian Boating Federation Incorporated, Department of Transport and boat manufacturers read that gross weight to include motor, passengers and all equipment and that greater consideration be given to calculation of gross weight.
We, the jury, recommend that a compass be added to all boats operating at night.
, We- the jury, recommend that the book called
Safety Afloat" be made readily available to the boating public.
We, the jury, strongly recommend that more common sense be used on the operation of boats with respect to all waters.
The information previously given to the house by me may now seem to have been inaccurate in respect to the load limit of the boat in question and the weight it was actually carrying on the night of the accident. If I seem to have misled the house in any degree this was done quite unintentionally, and resulted from misunderstanding or lack of information on three points, which I am now glad to clear up.

(a)	The R.C.M.P. had interpreted the load limit of the boat as being 975 pounds exclusive of the power unit.
(b)	The weight of the clothing and equipment worn by the men was estimated at 8 pounds per man, a figure usually taken for this purpose. It now seems that the total weight of personal clothing and equipment may have somewhat exceeded the 40 pounds calculated by the police-we cannot as yet be sure of the exact weight.
(c)	A tarpaulin weighing 14 pounds 12 ounces, an anchor, and an anchor rope, are now understood to have been carried in the boat. At the time I gave my earlier statement, it was not known that the boat was carrying these items, and they were therefore not included in the police weight calculations, although they were in the figures produced at the inquest.
The police calculations upon which my statement was based were therefore as follows: Weight of men, 860 pounds, and I should say here that is the actual weight as established from the personal records and as produced at the inquest; weight of clothing and personal equipment was 40 pounds, making a total of 900 pounds, and leaving a 75-pound margin to cover other items of equipment in the boat exclusive of the power unit.
The weight of the other equipment at that time known to have been carried in the boat, exclusive of the power unit, totalled 52 pounds 12 ounces, and it was on that basis I said that the weight carried was within the 975 pounds maximum weight authorized.
It now turns out also that we underestimated somewhat in using the standard estimate of 8 pounds per man for clothing, etc., worn or carried on the person. Such items as one overcoat, revolvers, and handcuffs had been overlooked.
The previous police estimate on which my statement was based should therefore have been increased by the following weights as established at the inquest:
Extra allowance for clothing and
personal equipment	 15 lbs.
Anchor and rope	 20 lbs.
Tarpaulin	 14 lbs. 12 oz.
Total	 49 lbs. 12 oz.
On this basis the total actually carried will be seen to have been somewhat over the presumed limit of 975 pounds.
If, however, we deduct the three items of equipment not previously known but now presumed to have been carried that night, namely tarpaulin, anchor and rope, the gross weight is again reduced to 967 pounds 12

ounces, or 7 pounds 4 ounces below the 975 pounds then understood to be the carrying capacity of the boat.
But the main cause of the discrepancy was, of course, the interpretation of the words used as to the maximum carrying capacity of the boat. The jury itself found that the wording on the plaque issued was confusing on this point, that is as to whether or not the 975 pounds load limit shown was inclusive or exclusive of the weight of the power unit. The R.C.M.P. had taken it that the weight of the power unit was not included in this figure and evidence to this effect was given by them at the inquest.
The wording on the plaque is as follows:
This boat is built to safely accommodate under normal operating conditions a gross load of MAXIMUM WEIGHT 975 LBS. and an outboard motor of not more than
HORSEPOWER (Mfrs. Rating) 35 hp.
I must point out that the police wrote to the Peterborough Canoe Company, makers of the boat, as late as February 10, 1958, inquiring as to the issuance of a plate stating the number of persons the boat could safely carry and the horsepower rating of the motor which should be used. The company replied under date of February 11 and said that the Department of Transport and the Canadian Boating Federation were in fact working together with the manufacturers to arrange for maximum load and horsepower ratings for various boats. The company went on to state as follows:
It is our understanding that the plaques are now in the possession of the Canadian Boating Federation and we hope to have our supply in the not too distant future and would be very pleased to supply you with the necessary plaques to attach to your boat but it would be necessary for us to have the serial numbers of the two boats in question, and if you could send these to us at your convenience we would, as soon as the plaques are received, make out two plaques for you and you could attach them to the boats.
The Royal of 1956 is not the same boat as the Royal of 1957 or 1958 and it is more to the specifications of our 1958 Nomad. The Venus for 1957 and 1958 are identical and the rating on this particular boat is 975 pounds gross load capacity and 35 horsepower for the motor.
The boat in question in this accident is the Venus referred to in the above quotation. The plaques were in due course received and, on the basis of the phraseology used thereon as well as the correspondence to which I have referred, the R.C.M.P. concluded, and I think not unreasonably, that the 975-pound limit was exclusive of the power unit.
I have gone to some length in explaining these facts, as I should like the house to understand that the figures previously given were honestly computed both in the light
R.C.M.P.-Drowning of Five Members of the facts as we had them then and of the best estimates we could make at that time.
Turning now to the finding of the jury that the boat was overloaded and also overcrowded, there are a number of points touching on this issue which I think might be borne in mind:
(a)	When the boat left the mainland on its fatal trip the weather was clear, there was a light wind blowing and the water was only slightly choppy.
(b)	There was no apparent reason for the boat to be more than five minutes run from land at any time.
(c)	Corporal Smart, the non-commissioned officer in charge was an experienced, selfreliant N.C.O. and he had some time previously turned back from the same stretch of water when he faced what he thought was an unacceptable risk.
(d)	Corporal Smart had eight men under his control on the night in question and he had a responsibility for using these men as circumstances seemed to dictate.
Earlier in the evening his party had made four arrests for drunkenness, and it was his plan and his duty to visit Georgina island and check on conditions there later that evening. Just what action he would take was to be dictated by circumstances and by such information as might come to him. It is a matter of record that aside from arrests for intoxication, four people in the area had been convicted for supplying liquor illegally between March 14 and June 2, 1958.
I might add that these people were not Indians. This was the general situation that Corporal Smart and his men had to deal with and which took them to the southern lake Simcoe area on June 7.
I point out these factors not by way of objection to the jury's findings but to emphasize that there will always be times when a police officer may be faced with situations in which he must exercise his judgment as to what must be done to discharge his duty, even though that may mean the acceptance of personal risk over and above the normal. I emphasize again that Corporal Smart was experienced in these matters and was a competent and reliable N.C.O. with 11 years' service.
I should like to comment on two other matters which have been the subject of criticism in the press or elsewhere in this connection. The first is that headlines and editorials in certain newspapers create the impression that there was an untrained novice at the helm of the boat on the night in question. This is unfortunate, since in fact the evidence actually
1744	HOUSE OF
R.C.M.P.-Drowning of Five Members given establishes that Constable Farough was a well-trained, competent and experienced helmsman who had been in charge of this boat in these waters as far back as August and September of 1957. His training included the use of compass, map reading and how to tell direction by stars at night. Evidence was also given that this boat had carried five men on similar patrols on lake Simcoe in 1957 without mishap.
Second, it has been said that the boat in question was too small for a large body of water such as lake Simcoe. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police in carrying out their duties have to move their patrols from lake to lake and from river to river, covering hundreds of bodies of water in Ontario and indeed elsewhere. In order to meet this situation they have secured patrol boats which are light enough to move by trailer but at the same time sturdy enough to cover most of the stretches of water they need to patrol.
It is admitted, of course, that small boats have a limit when used on large water surfaces, but we also know that they can be operated safely along a shore line, in coves, bays and the like. It becomes a matter of judgment, therefore, keeping in mind the urgency of the duty, as to how far patrols may be extended on open water with the type of equipment we have. I repeat here that, when this patrol left, the water was only slightly choppy, and having regard to the speed of the boat it did not need, so far as we can see, to be more than five minutes from shore at any particular time.
While I have made these general comments, I wish to make it clear that the verdict of the coroner's jury is accepted and will be used to the fullest extent as a guide for the future. In particular I would emphasize the following points:
(a)	The coroner's jury found that the phrasing used on the plaques fixing safe maximum load and power limits is confusing. My colleague the Minister of Transport informs me that steps are being taken to improve the wording on these plaques so as to remove any possibility of misunderstanding.
(b)	The coroner's jury also found that the life jackets and cushions as used in this boat are unsatisfactory in case of emergency. These were standard items of equipment approved by the Department of Transport, and the Minister of Transport informs me that this question is being studied in the light of the jury's finding and the evidence given and tests made at the inquest.
(c)	The commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has set up a board of officers to review the situation in the light


of the evidence and verdict at the inquest, and to examine and report on what steps, if any, might be taken to reduce the risk that members of the force face in carrying out water patrols, and to ensure that safety rules consistent with the demands of police duties are always followed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house will welcome the statement by the minister, particularly in view of the fact that the findings of the coroner's jury were somewhat of a discrepancy with what the minister had announced earlier. I think, too, the house will join with me in deep regret that so many Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers should have lost their lives on this occasion. I believe this is the first time that so many of these valuable men have lost their lives on an occasion such as this.
It occurs to me that while the house will welcome the statement made by the minister, there is no doubt but that there has been a breach of the Department of Transport small boat regulations. I am wondering whether or not the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Transport will continue the investigation which I understand is being carried on under the Canada Shipping Act. I may have misunderstood the Minister of Transport when he answered a question in the house earlier but I was under the impression that an investigation, if not under the Canada Shipping Act then under some other authority in the department, was being proceeded with. The question which arises in my mind now is this. Notwithstanding the investigation which the superintendent of the R.C.M.P. is carrying on, will the Minister of Transport continue his own investigation, and what action will be taken in this case under the provisions of the small boats regulations?

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON DROWNING OF FIVE MEMBERS OF FORCE

Mr. Speaker, the members of this group appreciate the full and very frank statement by the Minister of Justice with regard to this very sad accident, and extend their sympathy to

the relatives of those who have lost their lives. I hope that as a result of this unfortunate accident the Department of Transport will commence some research into the production of a satisfactory life preserver for people in small boats. A good many of us have found from our own experience that the type of life preserver now in general use is totally unsuitable in cases of emergency, in view of the short time there is in which to put on these life preservers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CHANGE IN HOURS OP SITTING ON DOMINION DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned this matter the other day in the house, and I should like to pursue it a little further today. As this holiday which we celebrate on Dominion day is our only truly national holiday, I think we should give more consideration to the Canadian people than we are doing by delaying our sittings until 4.30 o'clock.
I mention the fact that members of parliament have other commitments. I notice the Prime Minister is not in his seat. I also notice that statements have been made on the radio and on television that he is participating in activities connected with July 1 in other parts of the country. As a matter of fact, every hon. member has been given an opportunity to do that, and we have had to refrain. Not enough consideration has been given to establishing July 1 as a truly national holiday for all the people.
Another important matter is the staff of the House of Commons. Every other department in the city of Ottawa is receiving a holiday on July 1, but those who work in the House of Commons and the people connected with the operation of the house have to be here. I think it is only fair and just to extend this holiday to a full day for members of parliament so they can play their part in the program that has been designed for our national celebration, and that the staff be given a complete holiday on that day.

Well, I have to agree that they had ample cause for rejoicing. I understand that they had quite a day at the Chateau Laurier. However, Mr. Speaker, the anniversary of our nation is much more important. I note that the Prime Minister was able to attend the Conservative victory; I also note with regret that our Prime Minister will not be' able to attend our national birthday celebration in Ottawa tomorrow, which will take place on the lawns of parliament hill.
This Machiavellianism is to be very much regretted. We had a premier in our province of British Columbia who for several years thought it was rather smart not to be attending to the business of government for which he was elected, but to be in other places. He and his cabinet were usually found all over the province making political hay at the expense of public services in the province.

I have noted in the press in recent weeks a matter to which all of us should pay attention, and which should be called to the attention of the house. I refer to the expression of regret that we still have not built up in Canada an understanding that, irrespective of the land in which we were born, we are all Canadians. To me and to our group it seems wrong that the one place that should give a demonstration of the meaning of the day is the one place where work will still carry on. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the motion of the Minister of Finance that the house go into committee of supply, I want first to take notice of the announcement made before the adjournment of the house at six o'clock on Friday last by the Prime Minister. It is true that the federal government and the government of the province of Nova Scotia have moved in with financial help to ease further contemplated lay-offs affecting about
9,000	coal miners, but unfortunately the assistance for the Dominion Coal Company does nothing to avert the 25-day mine shutdowns in Nova Scotia. It will do very little to provide additional outlets for the record coal stockpiles accumulated in the face of declining demand, stockpiles which are increasing daily since the present government took office. In fact it was clearly stated- and I want to quote the Prime Minister's own words as reported at page 1737 of Hansard of Friday, June 27, 1958:
Even in the face of those reductions in working days, the company has estimated, and that estimate has been confirmed by the dominion coal board, that by the end of the year 1958 there would be in stockpile 750,000 tons of coal in excess of the normal average carryover.
It is evident, therefore, that despite the action taken by the government there will be at the end of the present year a stockpile which will reach close to 1,400,000 tons, which will be practically equal to the carryover which the company has on hand today.
In view of the vast expansion and growth which has taken place the federal government decided in 1955 to appoint a royal commission to study Canada's economic potential in order that the Canadian people could be more fully informed of the longterm economic prospects of our country. The commission was appointed to study our productive capacity, the growth and distribution of our population, the production and nature of our industrial and social capital.
This commission, having as its chairman Mr. Walter Gordon, was known as the Gordon commission. In its preliminary report made public in December of 1956 a special paragraph was devoted to the problems and difficulties in the four Atlantic provinces. In this preliminary report it was generally recognized and made clear by the commission that there is no single or simple solution to the problems of the Atlantic

region. Besides transportation and communications, special attention was given to the situation of the Nova Scotia coal industry. This question received special attention, not only because of its importance to the economy of one of the Atlantic provinces, but also because of the great number of people who are dependent, either directly or indirectly, upon the industry for their livelihood. After all, it is perfectly obvious that in Nova Scotia alone a population of over
120,000	people, including 8,000 or 9,000 coal miners, would be affected. In New Brunswick it also affects the Minto area in York-Sunbury, where over 1,000 miners reside.
In addition, the 1946 royal commission on coal known as the Carroll commission had been assigned a complete and extensive study of this industry, including its mechanization, its productivity and management-labour relations. It recommended proper action by the federal government in order to improve, if possible, at all levels the operation of the industry including relations between management and the miners employed.
It is generally recognized that one of the main factors affecting this industry in earlier years, and in fact a problem which is also in existence today, is the competition from United States coal in consuming centres in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Previous governments accepted the idea of a subvention policy to ensure the survival of the coal industry. This subsidy on the transportation of coal was followed by the Maritime Coal Production Assistance Act, providing long-term loans to the coal companies for the modernization and mechanization of their plants.
In the past number of years it has been apparent that certain factors such as deteriorating market conditions caused by competition from other fuels were having unfavourable effects on the coal industry. It was then considered advisable to discontinue, for the time being at least, the mechanization program which had resulted in increasing the productivity in 1955 to a rate 47 per cent above the levels which had prevailed in 1945, output per man day of 2.33 tons as against 1.58 tons ten years earlier. This output per man day could increase to 3.79 tons by 1960, thus bringing our total production close to 7 million tons per year, with a present yearly market potential of 5 million to 5J million tons.
It was generally recognized that the main market for Atlantic coal must remain in the maritime provinces and that every effort should be made to retain and increase it, even to the point where this would necessitate

It was clearly indicated in the Gordon commission recommendations that such subsidy arrangements should be designed to encourage the use of Nova Scotia coal in the generation of thermal power in the Atlantic region.
In the presentation of his budget on March 14, 1957, the minister of finance, Mr. Harris, clearly indicated that it was the government's intention to launch an immediate review of the maritime transportation system in general, and thereafter put forward proposals as soon as feasible. The government initiated the notion of the interconnection of the Nova Scotia-New Brunswick electrical systems. The minister of finance announced that the federal government would be prepared to provide the main interconnection facilities within and between those provinces, and to build and operate such large thermal plants as might be needed either to replace existing ones, should efficiency so indicate, or to meet the requirements of growth and industrial development.
These were the terms of the general proposal made by the previous governmenl through its minister of finance on March 14 1957. This proposal opened the way for immediate negotiations between the federal government and the provinces concerned for the implementation of this offer. This program for thermal power plants in the maritimes was initiated for the dual purpose of providing additional power at lower cost and, at the same time, assuring a much needed outlet for maritime coal.

I stated that by doing what the hon. member proposed he would do inestimable harm to the long-range future of that same coal industry which every member of parliament from the Atlantic provinces, and which every party surely must support. If one looks at the history of the Atlantic provinces one finds that since confederation there has been a gradual decline because they joined with the central provinces in an east-west movement, and this was not in accordance with the natural geography of the area. They made this great sacrifice in the interest of building, on the north half of this continent, a nation in which we could have our own way of life.
When this party was elected in June last one of the pledges we made was to lift up those regions and those groups in Canada which had fallen behind the national standard of living. There was no question in the minds of the people of this country, because by our spoken word on many occasions we specifically mentioned the fact that the maritime provinces and the prairie provinces, through no fault of their own, had fallen behind the national level. One of the first things this government did, therefore, was to fulfil that pledge in so far as the maritime provinces were concerned by introducing the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. The fundamental purpose of this act was to provide cheaper industrial power to the Atlantic provinces. Cheaper industrial power is not obtained by any single device. It is obtained by using every device known to engineers and economists to reduce the costs. The question of interest, particularly in hydro plants, and the question of the type of fuel as applied to thermal plants, the question of

building transmission lines interconnecting the various power grids, are all matters one might mention in this connection.
It is a matter of great pride that today in the province of New Brunswick they are planning to transmit power to Nova Scotia, and they are planning to receive power back from Nova Scotia. They are also selling power to the state of Maine, and doing very well from it. They would like, in the future, to see power coming from Quebec. This power from Newfoundland will come into their area and they, too, will be shipping power back to Newfoundland. It is by means of this interconnection that you achieve these great savings. Savings are also achieved by the technique of "peaking", whereby you get your lowest costs by using hydro and thermal in the correct sequence to give you the lowest cost to industry. We are trying to do all these things under this Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act. I, as a member of a political party, am quite aware of the things that were said before the election of June 10 in this regard. I do know that the then minister of public works, Mr. Winters, made a deathbed repentance and promised to look into this matter of subventions.
That statement is not correct.

We did achieve that on a temporary basis. We have agreed to examine all this periodically so that any plant manufacturing electric power from thermal fuel will have the same advantage in any Atlantic province as currently exists in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

This is a very serious question and must be given serious attention. The reasoning I put forward is very simple. Our philosophy behind reducing power costs in the Atlantic provinces was to provide inducements to industry to use that capacity. It was on that one single point that the whole future development of the Atlantic provinces depends. If industry will come in, providing opportunity to work in the factories, there will be more demand for power. That has been the experience all across this country. Never in this country's history or, to my

But my department has the responsibility of looking ahead not just for two or three years but for 30 years or 40 years to see the future of this country and to make plans for the multiple use of our resources efficiently. As the minister responsible I naturally must look ahead those years in the Atlantic provinces. speechtext:
I happen to have a copy of the statement referred to and the words used are "asking and demanding" that coal be used in thermal plants. But what I am pointing out is this. We are asking and we are demanding that coal be used in thermal plants in the maritime provinces because we have full awareness of the needs of the coal industry in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick. But what I am saying is this. To insist in a general agreement that only coal should be used would be suicidal and completely destructive of the long-range future of the coal industry in that area. The reasons I am trying to advance are simple. If the demand for coal is as great as mentioned, we shall have full use of all the coal we know of in the Atlantic provinces area, and in addition we shall be bringing in, I hope, with the co-operation of Newfoundland and Quebec, hydro power over long distances; and maybe in the lifetime of many of us here-in fact, I would say in 10, 15 or 20 years-you will see large nuclear plants in operation in the provinces to provide us with the energy we need.
I think I have said enough to make it clear that as responsible people we are asking and demanding from the government of New Brunswick that coal be used in this present emergency because it would be wrong for us to be helping the coal industry on the one hand and to be slapping them down with the other. But to insist, in a term of a general agreement going over 30 years or 40 years, that only one type of fuel would be used would be to put that power commission or any other power commission in the hands of one supplier or the other.
I could point out many technical advantages to show that any plant can use both facilities side by side. There is a plant in my home city of Saskatoon which has three sources of thermal power which they make use of one after the other or simultaneously, namely coal, gas and oil. I point out that if you go down to the province of Nova Scotia you will find that the Dominion Steel Company, which is a producer of coal and which is trying to get rid of its surplus, has standby oil equipment for logical technical reasons, namely to reduce their cost and to make their plant more efficient to carry the power to the people that need it. Any person that examines all the facts will recognize the injustice, the complete crucification you would bring on an industry by insisting that for a 30 year or 40 year period one fuel should always be used when these other things are developed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, having dealt with this matter of coal, oil and nuclear
[Mr. Robichaud.l
power and hydro power in the province of New Brunswick and the Atlantic provinces generally, I should just like to make a few remarks in answer to what the hon. gentleman said at the end of his remarks. He spoke in terms of derision of the future that the Prime Minister envisaged, and he was kind enough to use my own name, and the hope of all Canadians for the future of this country. I think the term that has been used is "vision". I would just like to quote a remark or two on this matter. I have in my possession the speech delivered by my predecessor in this department, the Hon. Mr. Lesage, in which he lays down the policy of the previous government on this question of development in general. This speech was made in Toronto on December 13, 1956 and I should like to quote from it as follows:
To go beyond that, however, to try to impose an over-all blueprint, a "National Policy", as some understand it, for resource management-to do that is to depart from the facts of our national situation. I have suggested already why such a "master plan" must fail of its purpose. In a country as vast as Canada, with widely different conditions and with different problems in different areas, there cannot be a single and unified policy for the management of resources.
The fact that the British North America Act places resources under the control of the provinces is not a matter of accident or coincidence, it is rather a reflection of the basic facts of our national existence. Resource problems are generally regional problems or local problems and must be handled on a regional or local basis. Thus it is that the facts dictate, and our constitution requires, that our resource management be in the hands of the provinces. This is the framework and background in which we must see the problems of resource management and development in Canada. Accordingly, to advocate a "national policy" on a national basis as a responsibility of the national government is to misread the facts of our economy and the spirit and letter of our constitution.
Does the hon. gentleman agree with those views?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Those are the words of my predecessor in office and I am merely using them as an example of a policy that is diametrically opposed to the policy I advocate. I believe that statement by the responsible minister in the previous government lays down a philosophy which is foreign to the whole history of this country. We believe that the resources of Canada belong to the provinces and that we operate in the territories to the north of those provinces only in the sense that we hold them in trust for the people who will live there in the future. We also believe, as the very act which sets up my department instructs me to do, that it is the responsibility of the department to do planning for the most efficient co-ordination and use of those resources for all the people of Canada. That explains why this

government on many fronts is offering cooperative plans of resource development with each of the provinces in order that they may best be able to develop their own resources and best look after themselves. There is no question whatever of infringement on constitutional responsibilities. In fact, we lean over backwards in an effort not to force our will in any way at all even to the choice of roads or any other project on which we are co-operating.
I mentioned this speech as symptomatic of the thinking of the previous administration and I am now going to take the liberty of offering some advice to my hon. friends in the Liberal party. I am going to ask those hon. gentlemen to go back in their own history and read the speeches of men like George Brown and particularly the one by him published in the Toronto Globe one hundred years ago, in which he laid down a philosophy of agricultural expansionism and resource expansionism identical to that of this government. How unlike the narrow views expressed here today it is! As the years rolled on the Liberal party drifted away from that broad point of view. I invite hon. members to look at the record of the speeches of Mackenzie and see how cautious he was about approaching these problems. I urge hon. members to then look at the record of pessimistic statements made by Blake. I suggest to hon. members that they go back to their beginnings and read the words of men like Brown in which they will find an expression of the faith that made the Liberal party worthy of its great traditions. Or, if hon. gentlemen prefer a more recent example, I suggest that they look at the statements of Laurier and the record of his achievements in the opening of western Canada under the immigration policy he advocated. These things are in tune with the thinking of the Canadian people today. I ask hon. members of the Liberal party to forget the petty politics of the last 30 years of the Liberal administration in this country and to see Canada as I see it, and as I think all Canadians see it, as a nation which is manifestly moving towards a vast expansion and a potential population of 50 million, 75 million or 100 million with all groups and regions in the nation enjoying some measure of equality of opportunity within the general framework of the economic standards of the whole country.
I think if hon. gentlemen were to do that- remember their beginnings and forget the political events of the last 100 years-they would see the needs of this country as the ordinary people see them. They would not quarrel with this attempt to help the Atlantic provinces on a broad front and they would not bring in this petty little criticism in an
30, 1958	1761
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines effort to embarrass the government for the immediate advantage of any one group or another. If hon. members were to adopt this perspective they would find themselves in harmony with the thinking of the Canadian people of all political faiths and would perhaps ensure their return to this side of the house much sooner. But as long as hon. gentlemen opposite adopt the igloo to igloo attitude, the attitude that says the people of the maritimes do not count or the people of the prairies do not count, and that the ordinary people in all parts of Canada who look forward and try to see greater opportunities for their children do not count, then there is no future for the Liberal party.
I for one, and I believe most people who sit with me here, have grasped something of the challenge that confronts Canada today. Our quarrel with the previous administration is that it did nothing about it. On the contrary, hon. gentlemen of that party have expressed themselves in speeches in important places as being opposed to the whole idea of a national development policy and have repudiated the idea of a blueprint under which our resources can be developed on a national, co-ordinated basis without exploitation or waste.
I think the house will recognize that I have spoken without too much notice but when this question is raised and when the government is attacked on the ground that its national development policy is phony-I believe that was the word used to describe this measure to help the Atlantic provinces-then I am brought to my feet in defence of something that many of us hold very dear.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Gloucester, (Mr. Robichaud), I shall try to confine my remarks to those problems which to my mind are of immediate interest to the coal mining industry, the miners and the people of the maritime provinces. These problems can be classified under three different categories. First, the shutdowns and curtailment of operations to take place during the next two months in all the mines owned and operated by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation in the Cape Breton area and on the mainland; second, the threatened closure of further collieries; and, third, a problem of immediate interest which has been most adequately covered by the hon. member for Gloucester, that of the increased use of oil rather than coal in some of the thermal plants in the maritimes.
This is the first time in the post-war period that the miners and people of Cape Breton, Pictou and Cumberland counties in
1762	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines Nova Scotia have been faced with the shutdown and closure of mines as was proposed by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation on June 17 and which in fact have been put into effect as of June 23. The news confirming rumours of shutdowns and curtailment of operations in the coal mines must have come as a surprise to the coal miners and the people of Nova Scotia because it is not so very long ago that such rumours were denied. In fact, during the months of February and March and even as late as the month of May this year the people of Nova Scotia were told that the industry was in good shape, that there would be no lay-offs in the coal mines of that province and that a new era had come to the maritimes.
At a press conference in Halifax which took place on February 17, and as reported in the Halifax Chronicle Herald on the following day under the title, "No Cut Backs in Coal Production", Mr. Allan C. MacDonald, chairman of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation's management committee and executive vice-president of A. V. Roe Canada Limited, is reported as having said that the company was banking on an "expected upturn in the general climate" and the "success of an aggressive sales campaign to capture a greater share of the Canadian market now supplied by United States coal mines".
Mr. MacDonald is reported as having said:
"The company will continue stock piling coal to maintain a high level of employment and is appealing to its mining force to continue its high production." He added: "The bank of coal on the surface now warrants shutting down of some operations, but we are not going to do it. We want the miners to keep on with their good job and will do everything we can to sell the production."
To Mr. Tom MacLachlan, president of district 26, of the united mine workers union, this statement was heartening. As reported in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of February 18, following the above mentioned statement of Mr. MacDonald Mr. MacLachlan had this to say and I quote:
We are certainly heartened by the report and the assurances of continued high employment in the foreseeable future. The co-operation of the miners and the operators . . . will continue and we are all looking forward to a growing of the coal industry in Nova Scotia. The policy of the company . . . eliminates a costly process of unemployment in the industry. It calls upon governments to take stock of the co-operation between the miners and the operators and to lend whatever assistance possible to see that the banks of coal will be shifted and eliminate possibility of slack times.
Commenting on the statement of Mr. MacDonald, the provincial minister of mines, the Hon. E. A. Manson, had this to say, and I quote:

The announcement was cheering and welcome to the miners, the government and the people of Nova Scotia. The approach to the coal problem by the company showed courage and optimism . . . for which it is to be congratulated.
You will notice also, Mr. Speaker, that this announcement by the company came at a most opportune time from the point of view of the electoral chances of the Progressive Conservative party in Nova Scotia. The announcement was given wide currency. There is little point now in saying it was wrong, and that cutbacks have taken place. Also, in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of February 18, in an insert in the "no cutbacks in coal production" article, and I quote:
Toward the end of his 90-minute speech in the legislature last night, Premier Stanfield referred to the DOSCO announcement regarding continued full employment in the province's coal mines.
He said it was a magnificent and appropriate stand for the firm to take, and the government would co-operate with DOSCO in every respect to the full exploitation of new markets for coal.
We are justified, Mr. Speaker, in asking this question now:	where are the new
markets? We also ask whether Mr. Stanfield may not feel he was hasty in lending his own weight to assurances given last February that no cutbacks would take place.
In a Canadian Press dispatch from Glace Bay which appeared in the Calgary Herald of February 25, 1958, Mr. Harold Gordon, vice president of Dominion Coal Company and general manager of all DOSCO operations, in an interview which took place in his office at Sidney, is reported as having said this regarding the industry, and I quote:
Mr. Gordon said the industry's position now is better than it has been for a good many years.
"We had daily outputs last year which were the highest since 1940. Last year we sold every pound of more than five million tons we produced."
Mr. Gordon also explained that the proposed $30 million maritime thermal power system promised a new market for coal. "It will be a considerable help to the coal industry when everything proposed goes into effect", said Mr. Gordon, "and we will put ourselves into a position to supply all the coal needed."
As late as May 23, the company denied the rumours of lay-offs and cutbacks. In an article of that date under the title "Plan no Cut Backs" the Halifax Chronicle Herald had this to say, and I quote:
Although a 800,000 ton coal stock pile in Sydney continues to pose a serious problem no working force of operational lay-offs are planned in DOSCO coal mines, A. C. MacDonald, chairman of the corporation's management committee told executive officers of district 26 united mine workers at a conference in Sydney, Thursday.
Mr. MacDonald told the united mine workers delegation there would be no slackening of operations at the present time but did not minimize the urgency of obtaining new coal markets. Indications are that new Ottawa assistance in coal marketing

will be sought and union district president, Tom MacLachlan, Glace Bay, contended that additional federal government subventions could add more new markets in Ontario and dispose of the mountain of more than 800,000 tons of coal banked here.
Mine union officers questioned Mr. MacDonald, who was accompanied by DOSCO coal chief H. C. M. Gordon, and manager of public relations Arnold Paterson, about a question asked in the House of Commons Friday concerning possibility of 25 days idleness in Cape Breton Mines.
Mr. MacDonald said there has been no change in the company policy announced in Halifax February 17 when he said "there would be no colliery shutdowns" in the foreseeable future, and every effort would be made to gain new markets.
The DOSCO management committee chairman, assured the union executive that if it is necessary to increase their coal carrying fleet of eight ships, this would be done immediately if market conditions warranted it.
I ask you to take note, Mr. Speaker, that this was on May 23, 1958. The predictions of the officials of the company as to the position of the industry, the denials of possible shutdowns by the authorities and the forecasting of a new era in the coal mining industry of the maritimes by the Conservative politicians did not turn out to be very accurate.
On May 31, the Financial Post reported that the federal cabinet had already under consideration a request from the Dominion Coal Company for government backing for a loan to cover the 1958 operations. It was stated that DOSCO was in urgent need of funds to help maintain its planned rate of operations until it could collect payments for this year's delivery.

Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order. The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) and I have several times during the present session- there is nothing personal about this-drawn attention to hon. members reading speeches-
On what side of the house?

From this side of the house we have drawn attention to hon. members reading speeches. Allow me to speak on a point of order, if you will. Mr. Speaker, may I draw your attention to Beauchesne's parliamentary rules and forms, fourth edition, citation 144, which says:
It is a rule In both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally, and not read from a written, previously prepared speech, for the reason that, "if the practice of reading speeches should prevail, members might read speeches that were written by other people-
We, of course, think that this is true.
-and the time of the house be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who were not deserving of their attention."
Specifically, we believe that these speeches are not only being read, but they are being

My point is that the former member for Inverness-Richmond has been replaced. My point of order is that the reading of speeches is against the rules of order.

On the point of order raised by the hon. member, I must say to him I have some notes with me and I am following those notes.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has no right to say that I did not prepare my speech. On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I also wish to say something in connection with the remarks by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris). He mentioned my speech. My speech was prepared by myself on Saturday and Sunday. This is the second time this has happened in this house. It might be better if the hon. member looked at both sides of the house and then he would know what to say.
Mr. Speaker, if an hon. member wishes to speak in this house he should speak from his own seat.

This question has been raised a few times by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) and the hon. member who spoke a while ago, that some members are reading their speeches. I admit it is a fact that we should not read our speeches. If hon. members wish to insist on it, I say that they should not read speeches from their side and even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will not read his speech next year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
First of all, I must bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that they are not permitted to raise a point of order on a point of order. I must furthermore remind hon. members that they cannot accuse other hon. members of reading speeches which have been prepared by other people. This cannot be done unless definite proof is actually available.
Further, on this question of reading of speeches this matter has been brought to the attention of the house quite frequently during recent weeks. The quotation which the hon. member read from Beauchesne is quite right, that speeches must not be read. However, a certain discretion is always given in the reading of speeches because obviously
1764	HOUSE OF
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines in some instances it would be impossible for some hon. members to make a speech unless they extensively consulted the notes in hand. The fact remains that, as has been said previously, hon. members are permitted more from a general acceptance than from anything else to consult their notes, but this practice of reading speeches in their entirety must stop at one point, and I believe this point has really arrived, and it will be my unpleasant duty to call to order members on both sides of the house from now on who read their speeches in their entirety.

Mr. Speaker, just before the hon. member raised the point of order I was saying that on May 31 the Financial Post reported that the federal cabinet had already under consideration a request from the Dominion Coal Company, and I was starting to say that at that time it was reported that the stockpile of 1.4 million tons was somewhat larger than usual but that it was sold or at least covered by firm orders. It was further stated that the company had a very satisfactory fleet of ships and that it was moving the coal as rapidly as possible to Quebec river ports. The need of funds was only to cover this lag in payments.
Then, in another Canadian Press dispatch, as it appeared in the Ottawa Journal of May 24 last, the Cape Breton Post was reported as having said that a decision with far-reaching effects on the maritime coal industry was to be made by the federal cabinet within the next 10 days. The Cape Breton Post, in anticipating such a decision from the cabinet, is reported as having stated:
"A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited, which now controls the Dominion Coal Company through the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, has proposed a 20-day layoff in all collieries in addition to the five-week production cuts already announced", the newspaper says. "Roe also proposed permanent closure of two mainland mines and one in Cape Breton.
To avert these moves the government was asked to grant the company a loan of major proportions designed to carry the industry through the next two years," the Post says.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, rumours were to the effect that the company needed help only for the balance of the current year; that a request was before the government for consideration, and that such help was considered sufficient to maintain operations as they were planned and, also, what is more important, at that time there was no mention whatsoever of any kind of lay-offs. Three weeks later shutdowns and curtailments were ordered and put into effect. Now that the shutdowns and curtailments are in fact a reality we are told that the company will need


government backing for two years unless additional lay-offs are made and permanent closure of three mines takes place.
If what I have just said is factual, there are a few questions which need to be answered. Why was the public not informed about what was happening? Why were the miners given to understand last February, and then again in May, that no idle time was contemplated? What happened during those three weeks between May 31, when the first rumours came out that Dosco might be in need of help from the government, and June 23 when lay-offs started to take place? During that period did the company really put its problem before the government? Was it made clear to the government that unless some help was forthcoming there would be immediate lay-offs at the mines? Was the company turned down because it was felt that those demands were exaggerated?
We were told by the Prime Minister on Friday that a suitable arrangement had been made between the government of Canada, the provincial government and the company whereby assistance would be provided in order to avert additional lay-offs and permanent closure of three mines, as previously announced by the company.
The statement of policy as outlined in the House of Commons at six o'clock on Friday by the Prime Minister reads as follows, and I quote from page 1738 of Hansard:
After full consideration and on the recommendation of the minister of mines the government has decided that in order to help maintain employment the subvention policy now in existence will be extended so as to include among the cost audit items to be determined by the controller of the treasury the amount of the insurance stockpile and interest charges of the excess coal stockpiled this year and the government of Nova Scotia has agreed to share in these additional costs with the federal government. I am glad to report that this action will result in the company being enabled to maintain at a high level employment in the coal mines it operates.
Earlier in his statement the Prime Minister said, as found on page 1737:
Even in the face of those reductions in working days-
The Prime Minister was talking about the immediate 25-day lay-off in addition to the period of regular holidays with pay.
-the company has estimated, and that estimate has been confirmed by the dominion coal board, that by the end of the year 1958 there would be in stockpile 750,000 tons of coal in excess of the normal average carryover.
The Prime Minister also stated:
-company officials undertook that at the end of the 25-day lay-off already announced the company would continue its normal operations providing it

is compensated for the additional cost to which it would be put to maintain the excess over and above the normal stockpile.
The newspapers of Saturday, following the statement made by the Prime Minister, reported that an unofficial estimate of the total cost of the measure announced by him would be $500,000 and that four-fifths of the cost would be borne by the federal government and one-fifth by the provincial government. It was also reported in the same Canadian Press dispatch that the scheme parallels the assistance given to the Britannia mine in British Columbia. If this is so, I hope that the end results in the coal mines of Nova Scotia will not parallel those of the Britannia mine.
The announcement by the Prime Minister on Friday presumably will have the effect of avoiding lay-offs after the period of the 5-week shutdown until the end of December, 1958. All that the Prime Minister did was to look after the company's charges on the stockpile in order to prevent shutdowns in the period from the middle of September to the end of December. For this the coal miners of Nova Scotia and the people generally are certainly grateful but, we wonder what will happen after December 31, 1958. Are we to understand that the government will extend assistance after December 31, 1958? We were led to believe that the company really needed assistance for two years in order to be able to keep production going and to avoid lay-offs.
We realize the importance of the coal mining industry. Possibly the hon. member who interrupted me a few minutes ago was not aware that I am interested in the mining industry, whether it be coal mining, gold mining, copper mining or zinc mining. I am also as much interested in the people of his own province because after all they are Canadians. Let me tell the hon. member that in my home town of Malartic there are many people who came from Nova Scotia in 1929 and 1930 to work in our mines. All of them are my best friends. They were called Nova Scotians but they were good miners and they were welcome in my constituency. They were welcomed to Malartic. They were strong, hard working men and they are still living in the province of Quebec. They have been there for the last 20 or 25 years and we are glad to have them with us.
Therefore if I take the opportunity today to talk about coal mines it is because I am interested and also because I know something about them. I know very well that if the government does not do something very soon the coal mines of Nova Scotia as well as the coal mines of the west will have further trouble.

The minister who preceded me wanted us to forget the political events of 100 years ago and then in the same breath he said that we should go back to Laurier. He did not want us to go back 100 years. He wanted us to be realistic. Let me tell him that the previous government was realistic and did a lot to help the coal mines. The dominion coal board was organized. Subventions were paid to the coal mines for the transportation of coal. Different research branches were organized.
It is true that the present government increased the subventions but now that they are in power it is their duty to do more for the coal mines. They told us in the past that we did not do enough. Now it is up to them. It is their duty and they promised the people of the maritime provinces that they would do something. We leave it up to them now and we hope that they will do something not only for the coal mines of the maritime provinces but for all the Canadian coal mines spread across the country.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise this afternoon and speak on the amendment. First, may I say to the hon. member who has just sat down that I welcome his interest in the Nova Scotia coal mining industry as I am sure all members from Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Canada do. Furthermore, may 1 say that I welcome the new look of the Liberal party toward the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia, the fact that they now realize that there is a coal industry in Nova Scotia and have some suggestions to make about it. Such an attitude was certainly lacking during 22 years they were in power and the economy of Nova Scotia is certainly the worse off for it.
The hon. member made some mention of some of the things that his party had to say about the Nova Scotia coal mining industry when the Liberals were in power. I should like to put certain remarks on Hansard as to what his party did feel about the industry. I should like to quote first from an editorial published in the Fredericton Gleaner of January 23, 1958. This is part of the then prime minister's (Mr. St. Laurent) statement regarding the coal industry and has reference to some of the facts that were put to him leading up to his answer in that regard. This is what Urwick Currie Limited had to say about Nova Scotia industry as found in the report of the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects:
The principal producers of coal in Nova Scotia are carrying out an extensive program of mechanization. It is expected that this program will be completed in 1960. It is estimated that the mechanization of the mines will result in a substantial increase in output per man-hour. This means according to estimates contained in our study

Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines on the Nova Scotia coal industry that if there were no reduction in employment, an additional two million tons would be produced each year. On the other hand, if production is not increased the services of some 4,000 out of the 11,000 mineworkers presently employed will not be required.
What was the answer of the former prime minister to that? Let us examine his answer in the light of that situation. Mr. St. Laurent, in his Fredericton speech, was referring to the proposal pulled out of a hat by Mr. Winters just before the June 10 election campaign with relation to assistance to the economy of the maritimes by thermal power. Mr. St. Laurent said:
Now, will maritime coal continue to be the cheapest fuel for the production of power for all time? I do not think it will. I think that coal is going to become more valuable for chemical and synthetical processes than it will be as a fuel. In the meantime, of course, we want these coal mines kept in operation because we do not want the coal mining towns to become ghost towns. But so far as I am concerned, so far as my opinions may carry weight in the decisions that are taken, we are not going to encourage substantial increase in the production of coal because I do not think that that would be fair to future generations of Canadians.
May I ask there, I wonder how fair it would be to the 120,000 people in Nova Scotia who are dependent on the coal industry.
What is the present government doing?

I will tell you what the
present government is doing my friend. If you gentlemen had done what you should have done when you were setting over here, you would not be over there now. We would not have shut you out in Nova Scotia because you never did anything for us.
That is a poor reply.

I go back to the quotation
from Mr. St. Laurent:
But so far as I am concerned, so far as my opinion may carry weight in the decisions that are taken, we are not going to encourage a substantial increase in the production of coal because I do not think that that would be fair to future generations of Canadians. I do not think it is fair to future generations of Canadians who will know they did not benefit from the greater value.
In other words, as the editor says, the coal should be left in the ground.
That is not what Mr. St. Laurent said.

I did not say that is what
Mr. St. Laurent said, but that is the conclusion reached by this editor and, so far as I am concerned, I join him in that conclusion.

I wonder if the hon.
member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) would permit a purely factual question?

I should like to finish my
speech. Since I have been in this house I know that the hon. member has been on his feet more than he has been in his seat, and when you sift what he has said you find that it all adds up to nothing. I do not feel I want to be disturbed.
I should like to make reference to another former minister in the government, the Hon. Mr. Sinclair. In Nova Scotia, he made a statement that the uneconomical coal mines should be closed and the people should be shifted to Ontario. That is a different story from the one the hon. gentlemen in opposition are now telling. What is the reason? The reason is that the people in Nova Scotia have shown the members of the opposition what they thought of their policies in the past. May I add a further remark at this time? The maritimes have indicated very clearly to the rest of Canada that they want the Progressive Conservative party in power because the Conservatives are going to see that maritime children can remain at home and have the same opportunities as any others in this great country.
Certainly, the coal miners can stay at home for the next five weeks.

I am not referring to Newfoundland because I consider Newfoundland has not been a part of Canada long enough to realize the difference between Liberal promises and Liberal action. As soon as they find out, they will get rid of the Liberals.
They have no place to go for work now.

These hon. gentlemen across the way have said that we never did anything or we have not done enough or we have not done this or that. Let me say this. This long sheet of paper contains all the things the Conservative party has done for the Nova Scotia coal industry. Let me say further, that the people of Nova Scotia did not forget that. They showed they remembered on March 31, and they will show it a great many more times in the years ahead.
Phony promises.

The hon. member can talk about phony promises. I grew up in an area about which the Liberals made many phony promises. Let me quote something from the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. This will give a little

Mr. Speaker, this amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) will give all hon. members an opportunity to express the regret which I am sure we all feel that, in spite of the measures announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) last Friday, there will still be a shutdown in the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia for five weeks. The Prime Minister's statement was greeted with warm applause, but I believe that applause was given spontaneously before hon. members realized that the measure did nothing more than postpone this problem to some future date. Certainly all the measure announced was that the cost of adding to the stockpile, together with the extra charges for carrying that stockpile, would be met and that, as a result of this provision, there would be no further shutdown beyond the five weeks as already announced and which will continue in spite of the measures.
If these measures could have been announced a little earlier there is no reason why this five weeks' close-down should have taken place. In replying to the hon. member for Gloucester the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) dealt with one point only. He concentrated on the fact that it might not be wise to write into an agreement a clause which would make it binding to use coal for a period of 30 years or 40 years in the future. However, he did nothing to explain the charges made by the hon. member for Gloucester that assurances had been given by company officials and by the premier of Nova Scotia and other members of the legislature that this shutdown would not take place. Neither did he explain the statement made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Comtois) some time ago that this stockpile of coal had been sold and was only awaiting transportation.
If the miners received cold comfort from what the Prime Minister said on Friday last, they must get even less comfort from the

words of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in that he asked them just to be patient and just to think of the great vision in 30 years' or 40 years' time, that we are going to get a great steel industry up in the north and that will make up for all the trouble and suffering which they are going to undergo at the present time.
This stockpile or this overproduction represents a reflection of the decline in our economy. If we are going to find a solution to that decline, surely the solution must be three-fold. In the first place, an effort must be made to stimulate our present business firms which are suffering from a decline and to get them expanding again. In the second place, new industries must be developed. In the third place, efforts must be made to increase our markets for coal. The blueprint for this industrial expansion has been drawn up by different bodies. It was laid down by the premiers of the Atlantic provinces in a conference which they held in Charlottetown last September. Prior to that, I think in last March before the election, the Conservative candidates for the Atlantic provinces met in a conference in Moncton and produced what I suppose they regarded as a new Atlantic charter. That charter was referred to in the July, 1957 issue of the Atlantic Advocate as consisting of seven resolutions which for the convenience of hon. members I should like to put on the record. They are headed "The Atlantic Resolutions" and they read as follows:
1.	A national development program of federal assistance for developing the resources of the Atlantic provinces, having regard to their differing needs and varying financial capabilities.
2.	Industrial decentralization, by placing a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures within the Atlantic provinces; by the establishment of crown corporations; and by encouraging private enterprises to locate in the area and to encourage the processing here of our natural resources as a result of special fiscal considerations.
3.	Atlantic provinces power development by means of financial assistance for the development of low-cost electric power which would fully preserve the rights of the provinces to build and operate both thermal and hydro installations and transmission lines and by immediate subvention on coal produced in the region and used for generating electric power therein.
4.	Adjustment of freight rates and provision of transportation facilities to allow our producers reasonable access to the markets of Canada.
5.	Capital projects program to provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area.
6.	Special adjustment grants for all provinces with a per capita income substantially below the national average. The claims of Newfoundland to better financial terms should receive recognition.
7.	The establishment of a Canadian coast guard.
I submit that this is a very fine blueprint for the development of the Atlantic provinces

but a year has now elapsed since this government took office and we have yet to see anything done for the maritime provinces beyond the special grants which were made at the last session. As indicated in these resolutions the federal government can do a great deal to assist in the development of the Atlantic region. Reference was made in the throne speech to the setting up of a small branch in a government department for advice to small businessmen. I believe this would be a very good move but when and if it is done I would suggest it would require much more than just a small office with two or three advisers. If that organization is going to be of any effect it should be organized on a regional basis in very much the same way as the national employment service is now organized.
There are some things which the Atlantic resolutions did not refer to and better communications is one of them. This is something that is absolutely essential if we are to develop our maritime industries. Transportation has been referred to and that is perhaps our greatest handicap particularly in Newfoundland. In spite of subsidies and special freight rates, transportation costs are a millstone around the necks of all small industries in the Atlantic provinces.
Something should also be done to encourage investment and that would require special tax concessions and depreciation allowances. More can be done than is being done at the present time to encourage the local industries we already have. We have many fine small industries in the maritimes which produce products of an excellent quality which could be utilized by the government in its construction programs. I have referred to some of these on other occasions. In Newfoundland we produce first class cement, fibre board and birch veneer, all of which is of a high standard. In the maritimes we produce excellent brick, aluminum windows and doors and other products which could be given special consideration by this government when it has purchases to make in its own building programs.
Did the old government do it?

The Department of Defence Production could also do much more than it is doing to encourage the existing industries in the maritimes. If the government intends to tackle this problem in earnest then defence production contracts should be awarded on the basis of factory prices. There are many items which we can produce at a lower market price than can be produced elsewhere in Canada but when transportation charges are added, particularly on the cost of products 57071-3-112

One of the prime requirements for industrial development in the maritimes, of course, is the production of cheap industrial power. Public bodies have an advantage in that way which I think should be permitted no longer. This could be done very well by granting tax concessions to private enterprises which are engaged in the production and distribution of power. Unless that is done the subsidies which are handed out by this government with one hand are taken away with the other hand in the form of income tax.
A third thing which could be undertaken is the expansion of markets. Of course this is a responsibility shared not only by the provincial and federal governments but also by the industry itself. This government has a responsibility because the coal which we are discussing today is a resource which is the property of the provinces. That resource should be converted into wealth while there is time to do it. The time will come perhaps sooner than we think when nuclear power
