will produce electricity cheaper than it can be produced from coal. Probably many hon. members will have seen the article which appeared in the local press a few days ago which said that before long this power could be produced at the rate of 6 mills. Once that happens the coal we have in our provinces underground will lose much of its value because its use as a fuel will go out of existence and other uses will have to be found in the production of dies, synthetics and chemicals.
When that day comes it will perhaps be a good thing for the coal industry, but we should be looking forward to that stage now and research should certainly be going on as fast as possible in order to find other uses for our coal. The time is running out when we can depend on it to sell as a fuel. Governments can help by using more coal to heat government buildings, and in thermal plants, as long as Canada is over supplied. The industry itself shares this responsibility with the government and I am not satisfied that in the past it has done all in its power to find new markets for coal or to expand existing markets.
As far as the Nova Scotia coal industry is concerned, it has had a first rate market on its doorsteps in the province of Newfoundland. We have been dependent on Nova Scotian coal for ages but the policy of the coal company was to take this market for granted. They did very little to expand this market and as a result, in spite of our increased population, the consumption of coal in Newfoundland has declined drastically over the last few years, although, at the same time, the consumption of oil has just about doubled. In 1953, the total receipts of coal in Newfoundland amounted to 275,000 tons, but in 1957, despite the increase in the population, it had declined to 258,000 tons, the latter figure including imports from the United States. On the other hand, 509,000 barrels of kerosene and stove oil were consumed in Newfoundland in 1953, a figure which had risen to 971,000 barrels in 1957, just about double. A lot of that imported oil could have been displaced by coal if our people had been treated fairly and if the company had done all it might have done to ensure a supply of coal of good quality at a fair price. But I have myself seen fishermen buying coal which was nothing but dust, much of which blew away when they took it out of their boats and still more blew away while they were waiting to get it into their houses. And for that they had to pay the highest price, between $25 and $35 a ton. A market cannot be developed when this kind

of service is given and I think the coal company must accept a good deal of the blame in this respect.
Speaking in this house on July 25 I suggested that coal depots should be established along the south coast of Newfoundland, because it would have been in the interest of the coal company to have found some means of distributing this coal at a fair price. What was happening at that time was this: our ships were going to Sydney and being tied up in Sydney harbour for up to two or three weeks, with all the extra costs of demurrage, waiting to get loaded. This demurrage cost was added to the cost of transportation. The answer to this problem would be to find some means of carrying the coal in a special ship whose cargo could be quickly unloaded, stockpiled at various points on the coast of Newfoundland, and distributed from the central points to the smaller harbours. This system, if it had been adopted, would have reduced the cost of coal considerably and instead of purchasing only one ton or a ton and a half- all they could afford-the fishermen might have been able to buy three, four or five tons at a time. The answer, if this government intends to do anything to maintain what bit of the market the industry still has, is to pay subventions on freight between Sydney and Newfoundland with regard to water-borne transportation. The former member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) raised this question in the house on January 14, 1958 as reported in Hansard on page 3317.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was referring to the opportunities of expanding the coal market in Newfoundland, and I had said that in order to do this it would be necessary to pay some subvention or subsidy on the water freight between North Sydney and our province. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself is aware of this need, as he is reported in the Halifax Chronicle Herald of May 3, 1957, as stating at Amherst, Nova Scotia, on May 2, 1957, as follows:
"What we want", he asserted, "is coal subventions within the province."

And again at Minto, New Brunswick, on June 1, 1957, as reported in the Montreal Star by the Canadian Press on June 3, 1957:
The Conservative chieftain speaking to party supporters in the coal mining community of Minto, New Brunswick, said "there should be and must be a subvention on coal transported within these provinces for power purposes."
Cheaper power for the maritimes and assistance for the maritime coal industry could be obtained, he said, if subsidies were provided for intermaritime coal shipments.
During discussion of the federal government's decision to join in the financing of coal-fired thermal power plants in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, Mr. Diefenbaker said the Conservative party's policy "is to give provinces a type of cooperation they have not had in the past."
Not only must subventions be paid on coal for power purposes but also for consumption in homes in Newfoundland if coal is to be made competitive with oil, which is being used to an ever-increasing degree, as I pointed out earlier this afternoon.
In my own riding there is an opportunity for expansion on the Burin peninsula where we have a considerable shortage of power at the present time. Not only are there large communities like Marystown, Garnish, Cres-ton, which do not yet have any electric power at all, but the fish plants and the mining operations at St. Lawrence are very greatly handicapped on account of the lack of cheap power. The St. Lawrence mines, like the Sydney coal mines, have been closed down. In fact, one of the fluorspar mines at St. Lawrence has been closed down now for over a year with 200 people out of work.
Then, again, there is the proposed development of the free port at Mortier bay. If this dream ever comes true a great deal of electrical power will be required, and that power is not easily obtainable in that particular neighbourhood at the present time. It may be possible to develop Hydro power at bay a'Espoir and transmit it to Mortier bay; but an economic survey might prove that' this power could just as cheaply be delivered on the spot by use of thermal units. Here again is a prospective opportunity at least for an expansion of the coal market in Newfoundland. It would therefore be to the advantage of both of our provinces if the federal government got behind this proposal for the development of a free port at Mortier bay.
As I said before, if the coal is to be used at all, some subvention must be paid on the waterborne transportation. I say that because their attitude towards the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia was very well brought out by the former prime minister in Fredericton, New Brunswick, when he said that coal was too valuable a product to burn and should be left for future generations to be used in the manufacture of synthetic articles. Therefore I am surprised at their attitude today which has been one of great concern for the coal miners. That was brought out by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) who had much to say about the problems of Newfoundland while speaking on the coal situation in Cape Breton. Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines been very little indication of a sound government policy emerging. It does appear to me that there is a statement made here and a contradiction made there. The country's business is being conducted on a day to day basis.
I would think there is no greater example of conducting the country's business on a day to day basis than this action which has been taken to temporarily relieve the problem that exists in the coal mines of Nova Scotia. I am sure that the people all across this country will appreciate what the government has done as a temporary measure. On the other hand, they will regret that something more could not have been done in order to avoid this five-week lay-off. Questions will arise in people's minds as to what will happen at the end of this year. Are we going to arrive at the same situation next year? It appears to me that some solution must be found without delay. After all, there are 9,000 miners affected and the total number of people affected runs to close to 121,000 people. Somewhere, somehow, if these mines are to be kept open, markets must be found for this coal. As the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) has said, there is a market next door to Nova Scotia, a market that could have been used to greater advantage in the past. I hope that when markets are being sought for Nova Scotia coal this will be one consideration.
We have heard a good deal lately about the policy of this government to divert 15 per cent of trade from the United States to the United Kingdom. The province of Ontario imports every year more coal than Nova Scotia produces. I would suggest, therefore, that if the government is serious about this 15 per cent switch in trade, they should switch some of the trade now given to the United States by diverting it to Nova Scotia. I recognize that there will have to be a subvention paid on some of this coal, but that has been done for quite a number of years.
This afternoon hon. members questioned what had been done by the previous administration. I am sure that anyone who wishes to turn to page 23 of the seventh annual report of the dominion coal board will find there the amount of subventions paid to coal mines over the years since 1928. This amounts to $80 million. I would suggest also to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) that he might check the statement he made this afternoon that these subventions were started under his party. In addition to these subventions which have been used we have also had money lent to the coal mines of Nova Scotia for the purpose of mechanization. This policy


was adopted as a result of the report of the royal commission in 1946. Up to date the money for this purpose has amounted to something over $5 million. I am sure that anybody would admit these figures hardly indicate nothing has been done for the coal mines of Nova Scotia.
However, we would agree that more has to be done if markets for the coal are to be found. Today the coal miners of Nova Scotia are facing the prospect of a five-week lay-off. No such lay-off has ever happened in the postwar period under a Liberal government, and I believe that if careful thought had been given to this problem last week a solution could have been found.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made reference to the fact that no such lay-offs occurred in the post-war period. I have just pointed out that within the last three years miners in my own mine have been unemployed for a three-week period because of a similar cutback. I am speaking from personal experience.
I suggest to the hon. membei that in the post-war period there has never been experienced in the history of Nova Scotia-
Who told you?
Would you care to know?
Yes, I would.

There has never been a case in the post-war period in which 9,000 men were facing a five-week lay-off. There has been a great deal done for the coal mines in Nova Scotia, but perhaps the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) does not want to admit it. I am sure that it is irrelevant who told me about the coal mines, but these mines have become very important to those of us who have been living next door to them for so many years.
The second part of this resolution deals with the fact that the government has backed away from its commitments to promote the development of industry in the Atlantic provinces. It does appear to me there would be something wrong in expecting any federal government to formally enter into business. However, I think three things can be expected of the government if they are going to be serious about the promotion of industry in the Atlantic provinces.
There are three things that I think could be done. First, I think the federal government should provide those facilities which

are within the authority of the federal government and which cannot be provided by the industry or the people concerned. Second, the government can create that atmosphere which is conducive to the development of industries. Third, it can increase, both at home and abroad, the markets that are required to sell the produce from these industries.
I am going to take a few examples from my own province in general and from my own riding in particular. I should like first to talk about the fishing industry which is the oldest industry in Newfoundland and which, up to a few years ago, was the most important one. It is not the most important one today but it is still an extremely important industry in the economy of this province. It is particularly important today because of the number of men who have been unable to find employment anywhere else and who now have returned to the fishing industry. If these men are going to be able to carry out their duties as fishermen they will need the assistance which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) is able to give. In order to develop this industry fully I would suggest that the Minister of Public Works increase or speed up the assistance which he is now giving to the fishing industry in Newfoundland in providing harbour facilities. This year, as far my riding is concerned, I am extremely grateful for what the minister has done but I believe that it could be speeded up in the hope of taking care of the large numbers of fishermen who have gone back to this industry.
The industry also requires the services of the science divisions of the Department of Fisheries. It is urgently in need of an expanded and more efficient bait service. This bait service, which we now have in Newfoundland and which was initiated by the commission government late in the 1930's, is one that has been able to assist the fishermen in getting to work earlier in the year and to stay at work later in the fall of the year and has increased immeasurably the production from this industry. Today, with the larger number of men engaged in the industry, the service as it exists is no longer able to give to all those who require it the service which they deserve. Here is another way in which the Department of Fisheries could increase the effectiveness of this industry.
Above all, this industry in Newfoundland today demands the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). There is in Newfoundland much disquietude concerning the markets in the United States, the markets in the Caribbean and the fish
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines markets in Italy. It may be, however, that there are those who feel that the fishing industry in the maritimes is not particularly important. Many of us remember when in 1957 the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) came back from the conference in London and was reported in a press conference on July 8, 1957 as follows:
Discussing Britain's participation in the proposed European free market, Mr. Diefenbaker said Canada would take a "benevolent" view of this so long as commonwealth farm products were not included.
He added that Britain also is inclined this way- though some of the continental countries are not- and that the U.K. realizes such inclusion would be serious not only for Canada but also for Australia and New Zealand.
Then a reporter said this:
He was asked whether he would include fish in the commodities that should be excluded.
"I don't think that's a very serious matter," he said.
May I now pass on, Mr. Speaker, to other ways in which the industry could be improved in the province of Newfoundland. The Minister of Public Works is very proud of the assistance which he has been able to give the industry of homebuilding, and I think rightly so. But while Canada has had a boom in home building, there has been no boom in home building in the maritime provinces. In my own province of Newfoundland there has been no regular boom. However, I agree with him when he says that the building of homes in Canada has a great effect on industry not only because of the amount of labour involved in building these homes but also because of the amount of labour required to provide all the things that are needed to build a home and to furnish it for those who are going to live in it. We in Newfoundland are able to supply fibre board, gypsum board of the highest quality, and a good quality of cement; and if orders were given to these small industries in Newfoundland to provide materials for the home building industry they themselves would be able to carry on to a far better degree than they are now able to do.
It is true that Canada is experiencing a recession but it appears to me that the Atlantic provinces are feeling a greater impact than is any other part of Canada. I might go on further, Mr. Speaker, and refer to my own home town. Here there is a paper industry which, before extensions were made to Powell river a year or so ago, was the largest integrated pulp and paper mill in the world. Here is an industry which pays out monthly in wages $2 million. Here is a port 30 miles from the sea which over the years has developed into one of considerable size and is comparable, for example, with Baie

This port is one that over the years has become extremely important to the west coast of Newfoundland. During the last ten years only once has the port frozen over the extent where icebreaking service has been required and that was in the winter of 1957. When the port freezes over and icebreaking services are required the cost of the product produced at Corner Brook is increased by 124 per cent. I am sure that hon. members who know something about the competition in the paper market at this particular time will realize the real importance of what an increased cost of 124 per cent can mean to the producer. With regard to encouraging industry in the maritimes, here is another way in which help could be given by providing all-year round navigation through icebreaker assistance.
Of course we in Newfoundland have always had the problems of transportation and it has been an extremely serious one for all our people, and particularly for small industries scattered around the coast. May I speak for a moment concerning communications and transportation in the province of Newfoundland? Over the years since confederation the Canadian National Railways has spent a large

It may be possible that at some time this railroad may be improved, as was referred to by the Prime Minister on April 5, 1957 when he spoke in St. John's Newfoundland and as reported by the Toronto Globe and Mail on April 16, 1957, when he said this:
Newfoundland's narrow-gauge railway should be converted to the standard gauge because the present line retards development, adds to the cost of transportation and therefore makes it more difficult for Newfoundland industries to compete in domestic mainland markets on the same basis as other provinces.
We have a tremendous communications problem in Newfoundland. The Canadian National Telegraphs has built an excellent communications system across Newfoundland connecting the larger centres. A good job has been done and I think they are to be commended for the service which they have rendered but it is now time to expand the service to other parts of Newfoundland so they can all enjoy the modern services of a communications system.
In mentioning this I might say just a brief word about television. Certainly television is important in the development of any part of the country. Tomorrow will be a great day for Canada and if there is one splendid way of celebrating the birthday of any country it is to present to the people of that nation something worth-while. Tomorrow, for example, there will be presented the St. Lawrence seaway and we shall also have a number of provinces entering into an agreement with the federal government concerning health insurance. These are great events for any country. Added to that there will be the opening of the microwave line that will bring television to many places across the country from North Sydney to Vancouver. In the year that has just past it is regrettable to me that an extra effort has not been made so that in opening this great television service Newfoundland could have been included. Newfoundland is the oldest part of Canada and it was here that the wheels of commerce and industry turned while the wind still whistled through the trees that stood on the site of every major city of this country.
I am going to turn now to the third part of this resolution dealing with coal being used in thermal plants in the maritime provinces. I remember very well the occasion last year when Bill No. 224 came before this house. One of the objections I placed before the house on that occasion was that the bill did not include provision for hydro power

lor the province of Newfoundland. I argued at that time that if any improvement was to be made in the supply of electricity in any province it was necessary to employ and utilize the resources which the province had. I pointed out at that time that although it was a wonderful thing for Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island to be able to receive the benefit of added quantities of electricity at a cheaper rate provided by their natural resources as a whole because they did not have hydro power, Newfoundland, where we have no coal but do have sufficient water power, should have been included in the bill providing for hydro power. The reason given at that time for the building of thermal plants in the maritime provinces was that it would provide, not only more and cheaper electricity for those provinces but would also offer a market for maritime coal. These two aims are very commendable.
Recently, however, we heard that in one of the plants that is to be built some form of residual oil which has to be imported will be used instead of coal. I listened very carefully this afternoon to the remarks made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). I can assure the house that he did not convince me with the arguments he used and I am quite sure he is not going to convince many of the maritime people with those arguments either. I was definitely under the impression, as were, I am sure, most of the people in the maritime provinces, that if thermal plants were to be built in that area they would use coal. I also recall that when members of the Progressive Conservative party were campaigning in the maritimes during the last election they, too, gave that impression. I have in my hand quotations from some of the speeches they made throughout the maritime region. The Halifax Chronicle Herald of Monday, March 3, 1958, reporting on a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) at Port Hood, Inverness county, on March 1, stated:
Dr. Smith answered charges he said he had heard made by Liberal speakers that the government has given no assurance proposed maritime thermal plants will be fired by coal by "offering my assurance that it is a condition of the agreement that coal will be used".

In my view this is a reversal of policy which is not going to engender very much confidence in a government that sees fit to make one statement prior to an election and changes its mind without any satisfactory explanation following the election.
During the past month we have heard a great deal about the vision of Canada that is held by the Progressive Conservative party. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if this is the kind of thing that is going to take place the so-called vision of Canada will be exactly what the word implies, nothing more than a vision. It will be nothing more than a figment of the imagination. Indeed, it will be little other than a cloud seen away out at sea, gilt-edged by the rhetoric of the Prime Minister during the election campaign, but one which develops into nothingness as it approaches the shores of reality. If we are going to have a vision for this country there must be something real about it. When statements are made in extremely flowery language there must be something behind them other than empty words. In the development of this country there must be real and tangible events. Industry must develop on the basis of reality. It can only develop if the statements and promises made concerning it can be relied upon. It is only by making statements with all sincerity and a firm resolve in carrying them out that we will find a basis on which to produce the standard of achievement for this country that all of us long to see.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion some of the most interesting remarks made in the debate today were those made by the Minister of Northern

Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) when he said that the policy of the government in relation to Nova Scotia is to use the coal of that province for the benefit of Canada in order that this resource which we have so plentifully in the maritimes will make the contribution it should to the Canadian economy. When the minister spoke of a great steel plant to supply the steel required by the eastern seaboard of the United States and Canada perhaps he was speaking of the hidden potential conceived by a beneficent nature which placed abundant coal resources in the maritime provinces. In the maritimes we have some of the world's greatest supplies of iron ore and coal. By bringing together these two resources we could use both to make a vast contribution to this nation without subventions or assistance from anyone.
I also listened with interest and some astonishment to the debate introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud). The biggest question I see in this debate is not whether coal will be used at Saint John but how the Liberal party after years of betrayal and neglect of the Atlantic region dares now to pose this question in this house when all Canada knows that such speeches from the Liberal party at this stage are nothing but crocodile tears.
I should like to take the house back for a few moments to a time not so long ago, to the spring of 1957 and the situation in the coal industry of Nova Scotia. As hon. members know, in Nova Scotia we produce about six million tons of coal a year. Of that production about 40 per cent is used in the Atlantic region, another 40 per cent finds a market in Quebec and southern Ontario, and the other 20 per cent is sold overseas. In the winter of 1956 and the spring of 1957 the outlook for our coal industry was very bleak indeed. We saw the St. Lawrence seaway coming to completion; we saw the natural gas pipe line bringing in gas from the prairies and the use of oil becoming more widespread across the nation. We saw threatened a market for two and a half million tons of coal that we had in the province of Quebec. The people of the coal producing regions of Nova Scotia were very worried. Certainly my constituency, which at one time had a flourishing coal industry and which still has five great undeveloped coal fields, was anxious about the situation.
But under the eyes of the last administration the coal industry was allowed to die; they acted as funeral directors and wept again their crocodile tears over the corpse of a once flourishing industry. We were facing a situation of a coal industry in dire trouble, of


pits being shut down not for 25 days, but for 25 years; a situation where no miners would be employed in Nova Scotia. We looked to the federal government of that time for some assistance to our coal industry, but not one word of help did we hear from them in terms of a subvention or something that would aid our recovery.
As it happens, a few years ago, at the instance of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, Dr. Christie had made a survey of the industry and had, in 1954 or 1955, filed a report suggesting a thermal power program, a system which would link up the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in order to produce cheaper power in the maritime provinces. As a matter of fact, the thing is not new because for over 20 years the Liberal government had been promising cheaper power to the maritime provinces. But cheaper power always meant subventions on coal to be used in power plants, and while they talked about cheaper power they would never give us the subventions. For example, in 1945 the then premier of Nova Scotia pointed out that in the aftermath of the war our coal industry would be in worse trouble than before and that we would have to have some power sources in the maritimes to give us cheaper power. At that time the suggestion was turned down.
Also in the spring of 1957 representations were made by the Nova Scotia minister of mines and industry, and by the premier of Nova Scotia, asking for subventions on Nova Scotia coal to be used in the power plants. Our province of Nova Scotia was ready at that time to finance and build power plants in Nova Scotia provided the government would assist them by granting the coal subventions without which cheap power could not be produced.
Finally, after 25 years or so of promises, on the eve of the election in 1957 the Liberal administration came forth with the so-called power program. As far as we were concerned, we wanted two things from a power program; first, we wanted cheaper power and, second, we wanted a market for our coal. When we first heard of this power program it looked like a new opportunity, a new life for the Nova Scotia industry. But when we began to examine the power proposal of the former government we found it very empty indeed; we found it would provide neither cheaper power nor a market for our coal. The more we asked the federal government to define its intentions and tell us exactly what they were giving us under this power program, the less satisfaction they gave us. Someone in this house used the expression "gobbledygook" a couple of days ago. We never heard more gobbledygook than

the Liberals used when they introduced their power program in 1957. One of the main questions as far as we were concerned was whether or not coal would be used in these plants. Now as reported in volume 3 of Hansard of 1957 at page 3294 the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, the Hon. Jean Lesage, had this to say, and I quote:
With regard to the fuel to be used by the plants that will be established under the federal proposal, the basic objective of securing power at the lowest possible cost is, of course, to be kept constantly in mind. This consideration will frequently affect the location of the plants that are to be built. It is, of course, also the desire of the government to see maritime coal used to the greatest extent possible in the plants that may be established.
In other words, this government wished to pretend to the people of Nova Scotia that it wanted to see Nova Scotian coal used in these power plants. But the minister went on to say:
The sharp increase in the price of oil and in charges for ocean shipping over recent months have resulted in a situation in which, over virtually all the maritime provinces, it appears that it would be cheaper to use maritime coal for the production of power than to use oil.
In other words what the minister was saying was that coal would be used only if it were competitive with oil, only if it could compete with residual oil from Iraq and Iran after the kerosene and other more valuable products had been taken out; oil which would always be sold at a much lower price than Nova Scotian coal. He went on to say:
There is some reason to think that this increase in the price of oil may not be as temporary as has sometimes been hoped or suggested. In the circumstances, the economic advantage of the use of maritime coal shows every likelihood of continuing.
With this statement the minister and the government of the day attempted to deceive the people of Nova Scotia into thinking that it intended to use coal in these thermal power plants when it is obvious to everyone that coal could never compete with residual oil; it is clear to everyone that coal could only be used if subventions were provided to move it within the Atlantic region to the thermal power plants.
They did not offer us cheaper power; they offered us power at cost. But we already had power at cost; we had the Nova Scotia power commission producing power at a big deficit every year. The power they offered us would not be cheaper power, it could easily turn out to be more expensive than the power we had then. Nor would the administration say that there would be a market for our coal, the second thing we wanted. We were completely turned down 57071-3-1134
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines by the Liberal administration, whose representatives have been speaking on this question in the debate today.
Let me take a little further this question of subventions on coal without which the power program would be useless. On page 3296 of the same volume of Hansard is reported a question asked by the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. At that time he asked, and I quote:
Has the government given consideration to expanding the principle of subventions on the movement of coal within the maritime provinces to assist in the use of that coal in competition with oil, assuming that the temporary condition may not continue and the price of oil may drop?
And the answer, given by Mr. Lesage,
was:
If the hon. member will read my statement he will find that I said or implied we did not consider it was necessary to give a subvention on coal so it would be competitive with oil.
I was going to say a deliberate misstatement was made, but I would rather say that the minister knew so little about the comparative competitive price of oil in eastern Canada that he could make a statement of that kind. But the important thing is, there was a flat refusal on April 9, 1957, a little more than a year ago, to give us subventions which would enable us to burn coal and to have cheaper power in Nova Scotia. Along with that we have the statement of the former minister of fisheries, the Hon. Mr. Sinclair, who said on a platform in Antigonish that uneconomic Nova Scotia mines must be closed. At the same time hon. members will also recall the report of the Urwick-Currie commission, which was asked to report on the relative costs of moving coal to thermal power plants or moving power along transmission lines.
This commission reported that it would be much cheaper to move coal to thermal power plants. They went on to say that so far as they were concerned, as a result of their survey, the production of coal in Nova Scotia would have to be cut to 5 million tons a year, which they admitted would displace 4,000 coal miners in Nova Scotia, and would turn
30,000	people dependent on those men out on the streets to seek their living. Still, we waited in Nova Scotia for some more clarification of the power program. We finally got it, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), when the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, came to Fredericton and there a few days before the election sounded the death knell of the Liberal party in Nova Scotia, and perhaps in the maritime provinces, when he said that his government did not intend to

They speak of a crisis in the coal industry. Yes, we have a crisis in the coal industry. We have had it as long as 1 can remember. Some people here have a longer memory than I, but I can remember all during my lifetime on Cape Breton island a crisis every two or three years in the coal industry. As I recall it, there was very little help which came forward from the administration then in power in Ottawa to assist men out of work and laid off in Nova Scotia coal mines.
What has this present government done? In 1957, a little over a year ago, our coal industry was on the rocks. We had been losing money, a lot of money, every year since shortly after the war. It was easy to be seen that before long our mines might have to close down without some help, and the 130,000 people of Nova Scotia who looked to that industry for a livelihood would have to look somewhere else, probably to the free tickets up to central Canada suggested by the Gordon commission.
This government, when it came into power in June 1957, immediately began a program that has saved our Nova Scotia coal industry. If it were not for that program we would not be worrying about this present crisis and a 25-day lay-off; we would be faced with the situation today where hardly a ton of coal was being mined or moved out of Nova Scotia. First of all this government made the power plant program a reality in terms of cheap power and in terms of a market for coal by providing subventions to move coal within the Atlantic region to those thermal plants. Without this subvention the power program would have been an empty gift.
Then, they gave us subventions to move coal into the Ontario market and above all to protect our market in the province of Quebec against cheaper transportation which United States coal would enjoy because of the St. Lawrence seaway, and against competition from that fuel in our natural markets. Further, they gave us something which the former government would never have thought of doing, namely the preference that Nova Scotia coal has in furnaces operated and owned by the federal government, to give us an additional market there. But, Mr. Speaker, I believe one of the greatest things that has been done, and something that


shows more than anything else the warmth of this government, of our leader and of his cabinet, and also their interest in our problems in the Atlantic region and also of their interest in the unemployment problem generally in Canada, was when we received the other day the announcement of the special help to the coal miners of Nova Scotia in general and of Cape Breton island in particular.
Hon. members know that we have 1,400,000 tons of coal piled up in Cape Breton. That is $14 million worth of coal. The Liberals insist that the 25-day layoff should have been covered by the government. The only possible way it could have been covered would be for the government to buy the $14 million worth of coal and try to sell it. They could not do it. No government could be expected to do that. They did the next best thing in an unprecedented move in Canadian history. Perhaps no other government on this continent or in any other place in the world would have given the co-operation and help to the Nova Scotia coal industry which was given recently in the announcement to pay the interest and carrying charges on that stockpile of coal, coal which can be sold in the normal course of events in the fall and winter of this year.
I think that all of the members from Nova Scotia in particular, and I am sure the people of Nova Scotia, give a great deal of credit to our minister, the Minister of National Revenue, (Mr. Nowlan), for guiding this tremendous provision through the cabinet, and for giving us help which by all the rules we could never have expected to receive. Then, we have speakers rise in their places who have the audacity to say, well, why was this not announced last week or the week before? I say that if they had come forward with a half decent program to assist the Nova Scotia coal industry five years ago we would not be in this crisis today. If the previous government was still in office, and if the same policies they advocated then were carried out, we would not have the thermal power program in the east today because we would not have had subventions on coal. We would not be running into the problem of whether oil or coal was to be burned in Saint John; it would not arise because we would not have the program. We would have thousands of men without work in Nova Scotia and nothing more.
Some reference was made to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Smith) when he spoke at Port Hood in the recent election campaign. Port Hood is in my constituency and I was with him on the platform that night, What the

Secretary of State for External Affairs said was that it was the policy of the present government that federal funds would be used for those thermal power plants only if the provincial governments concerned agreed to burn coal. That was the policy of the government at that time, the guarantee to Nova Scotia, and I understand that it is still the guarantee of the government today. The guarantee is clear, but if in the thermal plant at Saint John oil is used, then that plant is to be built at the expense of the province of New Brunswick. If it will use coal, then it will be built at the expense of the government of Canada.
Much mention has been made of the fact that the agreement did not specifically tie the governments of the provinces down to using coal. The only way that coal could be used, and the only way to provide that coal could be used, was, as has been done by this government, to provide a subvention on coal so that coal is competitive with oil in thermal power plants.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. We in Nova Scotia feel that we have obtained from this government more in a year than we have obtained from other governments since confederation. They realized our problem; they met it boldly and with a forward program. I say further that in Nova Scotia we do not expect that 22 years of Liberal neglect and betrayal can be cured in one year. There are still many problems but I am confident that this government will meet those problems and that the position of our coal industry in Nova Scotia and the position of our thermal power program are an awful lot better than they were a little over a year ago. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express very briefly the support of this group for the spirit, the principle and the purpose of this amendment which are to urge the government to do something to provide more employment for coal miners in Nova Scotia. In saying that, it does not include support for all the procedures suggested, or support necessarily for the remarks made by various members with respect to the present situation or the future situation.
We are supporting the principle and purpose of this amendment. I think the debate we have had today clearly indicates the lack of planning with respect to the development of our natural resources and the need for planning and an over-all policy in this respect. I know there are a good number of members in the house tonight who have over a period of 13 years listened to the former member for Cape Breton
30, 1958	1781
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines South deal with the situation, particularly at times when there were depressions in the coal industry which appeared to be periodical and not quite as bad as at present, when he urged upon the government of the day the necessity of a national fuel policy. I well remember him dealing with this matter in detail session after session during appropriate opportunities on the estimates and also in support of private members' motions moved by himself.
Here we are after all that time still finding ourselves in the same predicament. I remember the former member for Cape Breton South dealing with the situation in detail one night in the house. At the time there apparently had been some temporary improvement in the situation owing to certain subventions and things of that sort. I remember quite well his saying that if the government of Canada did not develop a national fuel policy the situation would grow worse and worse from year to year and the solution would be increasingly difficult.
I think that indicates the situation we are facing tonight. I think the whole debate justifies the C.C.F. policy and approach to this type of situation, namely the necessity for planning for a national fuel policy related to the general development of our natural resources, related to a financial and industrial policy that takes cognizance of all the facts and provides a program and policy as a result of the application of the best brains we have to a given situation free from the influence of certain private interests who, when they get into difficulties like this, throw their casualties on the public exchequer to take care of and also refuse to continue to develop their natural resources.
This failure on the part of previous governments-and I am not taking sides in this issue so far as free enterprise supporting the government is concerned-has resulted in no action, then limited action, with still considerable unemployment, sufficient unemployment to concern those persons who moved the amendment this afternoon.
This is not an isolated case, Mr. Speaker. While we all sympathize with the unemployed coal miners in Nova Scotia and are in hearty support of what the members of that area wish to do to improve the situation, this is only one instance of a number of similar situations in the coal industry in Canada at the present time. To illustrate, without being out of order, the greater compass of this problem than is recognized by many members from Nova Scotia, I will mention the difficulties of a little town in Kootenay East
1782	HOUSE OF
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines called Fernie. The American Coal Company-operated a mine there for nearly 60 years. The company made very large profits until recent years. Because of that operation a city was built with all the facilities that go with a city. With less than a month's notice to the city council and to the union concerned the company closed down the mine. They took out the machinery. I am informed that the mine contains reserves of coal sufficient for 50 or 60 years. There was no sense of responsibility to the community, no sense of responsibility to the miners, no regard for the predicament in which these people were placed. They closed down the mine not because they were losing money but because by keeping open more efficient mines they could maintain their rate of profit.

Surely it would have been perfectly simple for the government to put into this agreement a stipulation that coal should be used, not necessarily forever, but for as long as coal was available and there was not an alternative market for it.
I want to be fair about this, and I agree that circumstances might arise such as were envisaged in that perfectly proper statement made by Mr. St. Laurent at Fredericton, which has been so distorted in this house by hon. gentlemen opposite, that coal will become more valuable as an industrial product than it will be as a fuel. I do not believe that either the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources or any of his colleagues on the treasury benches are prepared to rise in their places and tell us that as long as coal is available for this purpose, and there is no better market for it, it will be used in the Saint John plant and in every other plant that is assisted by the federal government. If any hon. gentleman on the treasury benches is willing to say that I am sure my good friend, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud), will join with me in withdrawing the third part of the amendment at once. We cannot understand why this statement has not been made.
The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources spoke about the problem of using coal in thermal plants and suggested that in some extraordinary way it would not have been possible to use coal in the thermal plants which were proposed by Mr. Harris and Mr. Lesage because it would have been too expensive.
I noticed that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, in an otherwise straightforward and candid speech, was very careful to leave out the most important and authoritative statement that was made on this subject and that was the one made by Mr. Winters last spring with the full authority of all his colleagues to the effect that it was the policy of the government to keep the cost down to the cost of the lowest priced fuel, and that if in order to keep coal down to the price of oil it was necessary to give a subvention to the coal, a subvention would be given. That was the policy of the Liberal government. It was our formal policy, formally enunciated by the minister from Nova Scotia and publicly stated.

speechtext: It happened twice, did it not?

maintopic: NET REGISTERED TONNAGE OF SHIPPING USING PORT OF CORNER BROOK
speechtext:
Yes, it happened twice, and what has happened now? The great double-cross. Once the election is passed, once the voters can have no more say for several years, the real policy appears.
The other thing that is very puzzling to me is this: We were told when this legislation was before the house last June that it was a matter of the greatest urgency, a matter of extreme importance to the government of New Brunswick who needed to get this bill so that they could go right ahead with this power project in Saint John. What has happened? Half a million dollars, more or less, was put into the estimates last year for this purpose, yet none of it was spent. This year another appropriation has been made, yet no agreement has so far been signed. What has happened to the urgency? Why, last January, was it so urgent, and why, today, has nothing whatever happened? It does seem to me that before this debate closes some member of the government should tell us what is really going on about the Saint John plant. Of course, we do know that in the last 12 months there has been a marked decline in industrial activity, accompanied by a regrettable decline in the demand for electric power. We were told by the minister this afternoon in a burst of candour that this power plant at Beechwood, for which a large sum of the taxpayers' money is being pledged, is now exporting power to the United States. Perhaps this is one of the ways in which the government is seeking to redress its unfavourable trade balance of which we have heard so much.
But it does seem to me that we were not told last January, when this legislation was considered so urgent, that the taxpayers of Canada were having to put up money to complete a power plant to export power to the United States. We are told that now. That is another of the things that come out after an election, another of those things that would have changed the face of things a good deal.

I have here an editorial, somewhat later in date than those he regaled us with,
and somewhat different in tone. It is entitled "The Plight of Coal" and it is dated June 19, 1958. The first paragraph begins:
Dosco authorities now have served what is being taken as an official warning of their intentions to cut back on coal production, "over the next several months" and, although the notice has been carefully phrased to ease the blow as much as possible, it still has hit as disheartening and disappointing news.
It was just four months ago today that we were moved to applaud in these columns an announcement from the company that, despite the decline in demand and growing stockpiles, there would be no layoffs or other forms of reduced operations.
I wonder, if that announcement had not been made, whether the results would have been quite the same on March 31. I continue the quotation:
This official statement, said Premier Stanfield as he read it to a cheering legislature, was "magnificent". It was issued by the same man who now conveys the sad tidings of this week, DOSCO management chairman Allan C. MacDonald. And it was less than a month ago-on May 22-that he repeated this assurance to U.M.W. officials in Cape Breton. The present intentions are, perhaps, understandable in the light of the existing market conditions for coal, but should such hopes have been held out to the miners and to the one-fifth of Nova Scotia's population which directly depends on the coal industry for livelihood? It has made many people here wonder if there is even worse news from Dosco ahead.
On top of this there was the disclosure of the previous day, when federal government documents concerning its program of assistance for providing cheaper power in the maritimes were tabled in the House of Commons, that there was no stipulation written into the agreements with the provincial governments that coal would or should be used in the new thermal power stations.
It is evident that the editor of this paper is not much impressed by the arguments put forward today by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
I wonder if the leader of the house would tell us what he hopes to do tomorrow.
